# FIRST FIRE research review

Research cut-off: 14 November 2026. This review evaluates seven decisions a Space Apps judge, student or researcher can check against public experiment records. Six concern reported experiments. The seventh concerns a proposed lunar experiment. The case records include the actual evidence, a decision, the strongest qualification and a concrete follow-up. Each of their 42 design alternatives has a mechanism, trade-off and observable proof criterion. Their ordering expresses an editorial judgment about the decision a user can support today. It is independent of experimental effect size or NASA endorsement.

## Why these decisions matter

The challenge asks for an interactive SI-assisted dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets combustion findings. It specifies crew environments and points out that partial-gravity evidence extends beyond PSI. For a lunar-textile question, an experiment can match pressure and oxygen yet study an inverse gas flame with oxidizer entering through a burner. For an alarm question, a material can produce a measurable aerosol yet fail to cross a detector threshold. Returning these as interchangeable matches would answer a different physical question. [Flame in Freefall challenge](https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/flame-in-freefall/)

NASA’s May 2026 Engineering and Safety Center assessment estimates that material replacements would be needed in 70% of **assessed subsystems** for an 8.2-psia exploration environment. That percentage refers to the hardware subsystems in that assessment. It cannot be attached to the fraction of materials that burn, the probability of a cabin fire or the adequacy of a specific fabric. [NASA assessment, executive summary and report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20260003925)

The active NASA-STD-6001B Change 3 requires five standard-sized specimens for upward-propagation Test 1. All five must stay within the 15 cm burn-length criterion and produce no secondary flame propagation by burning debris. The research rigs examined below used different sample dimensions and outcome definitions. A five-second flame survival, a smoke measurement, an isolated airflow change and a successful hot ignition each answer a different question from the standard. [NASA standards record and revision](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/NASA/NASA-STD-6001), [§§7.1.2–7.1.4, PDF pp. 27–29](https://standards.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/standards/NASA/B-w/CHANGE-3/3/2025_06_25_NASA-STD-6001B_w_Change_3_FINAL_Admin-Change-FINAL.pdf#page=28)

## Experiments and counterevidence

**1. LUCI, slower spread and a longer-lived SIBAL flame.** In the New Shepard flight a 5 × 30 cm cotton–fiberglass strip burned downward, while a 4 mm PMMA rod burned upward. The apparatus rotated and both samples used the same atmosphere. For SIBAL, the paired ground/partial-g comparisons report flame-base speeds of 1.5/0.9 mm/s and flame-tip speeds of 2.8/1.1 mm/s. The flame-width comparison reports extinction roughly 45 seconds earlier on Earth. The individual flight fit gives 0.92 mm/s for the base and the comparison table rounds to 0.9. The rocket carried the experiment in a sealed chamber in simulated lunar gravity. The deck’s total burn duration across the experiment is a poor substitute for a specific fabric’s duration. [LUCI flight description, PDF pp. 4, 12, 16 and 19](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20250010653/downloads/ASGSR%202025-LUCI-Ferkul-Presentation-v2-20250010653.pdf#page=12), [paired figures, PDF pp. 32–34](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20250010653/downloads/ASGSR%202025-LUCI-Ferkul-Presentation-v2-20250010653.pdf#page=33)

LUCI’s ground comparison tracked a near-20% oxygen atmosphere during the SIBAL observation. In flight, concentration declined from roughly 20% to 18%. The investigators also describe less reliable ground tracking. These features preclude a universal duration multiplier or a claim that only gravity changed. An independent 20-second parabolic test of downward-spreading, 5-cm-wide SIBAL at 21% oxygen and normal pressure measured 0.86 mm/s base speed. A short centrifuge-drop experiment gave 1.1 mm/s. They strengthen the *early spread* comparison; their time windows cannot test a 45-second difference in extinction. An earlier poster describes immediate Earth extinction under its own conditions; use the actual paired LUCI run to answer the numerical duration question. [LUCI PDF pp. 23–27 and 42](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20250010653/downloads/ASGSR%202025-LUCI-Ferkul-Presentation-v2-20250010653.pdf#page=24), [day 2, parabola 29 and cross-platform rates, PDF pp. 21–22](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20260001966/downloads/Ferkul-Lunar%20and%20Planetary%20Science%20Conf%202026%20v2.pdf#page=21), [2024 poster record](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240015307)

**2. Saffire-II, what ignited at a material interface.** Sample 2-7 used a 5-cm PMMA lead-in and 24-cm length of Nomex HT90-40 with about 7 mm overlap. The PSI table lists approximately 22.1% oxygen, 20 cm/s concurrent flow, 80 W igniter power, 9.2 s igniter time and 140 s composite burn duration. Its phase-specific result is 5 cm PMMA consumed and zero Nomex burn length. NASA also describes significant damage to the first centimetre and blackening over the first five. Soot deposition is one possible explanation for discoloration. The assembly’s elapsed time cannot serve as either a Nomex ignition delay or a Nomex burn duration. Ground experiments with the same grade found that PMMA could support Nomex burning in ambient air until the external flame burned out. Rank support for the exact composite event separately from support for assisted or self-sustained Nomex spread in a changed atmosphere. [Flight report pp. 24–25 and Table I on p. 29](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170008805/downloads/20170008805.pdf#page=24), [PSI-99, row 8](https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-99), [Thomsen’s experimental study, dissertation ch. 6](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/01d5j8mc)

**3. FLEX, visible extinction and later chemistry.** NASA’s PSI row 156 records a 2.73 mm initial droplet, 2.52 mm diameter at visible extinction and 2.7 s burn time for FLEX-155. The technical report interprets the subsequent high vaporization rate, plateau and vapor cloud as evidence of cool combustion. Keep “investigators inferred” attached to that conclusion. FLEX-120 also produced a cloud, but incomplete diagnostics left cool burning inconclusive. Its row 121 records initial/visible-extinction diameters of 2.45/2.39 mm. The changed pressure, support and CO₂ fraction prevent treating these two runs as a controlled estimate of CO₂ suppression efficacy. A project that uses the same exact-quote checker for both captions must still make opposite decisions about evidence strength. [PSI-69 table](https://doi.org/10.60555/mbq8-0451), [FLEX-155, figure 159, viewer p. 189](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150023456/downloads/20150023456.pdf#page=189), [FLEX-120, figure 124, viewer p. 154](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150023456/downloads/20150023456.pdf#page=154)

**4. SAME, measured smoke and the likelihood of an alarm.** In §3.2 of their original study, Meyer and colleagues compare sensor responses against a dashed alarm threshold in Figure 9. The ISS light-scattering unit would have missed over half the tested Kapton cases and two-thirds of the Teflon cases. The same detector produced large responses to several other smokes. The Shuttle detector had fewer usable observations. Preserve each fraction exactly at the authors’ level of reporting: there is no basis here for a per-material denominator extrapolated from the total number of runs. In the PSI reflight table, runs 51 and 101 both list 60 s at the source but differ in inlet flow, heater setting and net aging. Their 60 s is a generation setting. The experiment does not supply a time-to-alarm for a lunar cabin. [Original study, §3.2 and Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/#S8), [NIST investigator account](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2018/05/nistnasa-study-shows-one-detector-doesnt-fit-all-smoke-spacecraft), [SAME-R table, rows 2 and 24](https://doi.org/10.60555/2np7-jv14)

The original §3.2 says **over half** for Kapton. A later NASA white paper summarizes that as **half**. The original authors’ result controls the case answer, and the later paper supplies context about deposition, filtration and design. A separate exact join is possible for SAME-R Teflon run 56 (CSV row 74: 8.1 cm/s inlet, 60 s smoke generation, 41 s net aging). Figure 10(a) explicitly shows an *unaged* Teflon subsample from that run. It documents particle morphology; the source offers no run-56 alarm classification in that figure. Recent detector work treats discrimination between smoke, cabin dust and lunar dust as a separate design objective and studies transport to sensors. [Original Figures 9 and 10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7918997/#F9), [2021 white paper](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210022143), [2026 NASA detector study](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20260005612)

**5. CFI-G, physical location of a gas measurement.** In the inverse configuration the chamber contains diluted fuel and oxidizer issues from a porous sphere. The 21202A1 and A2 rows both have 6% initial ambient ethane and 85% oxygen in the burner stream. The dissertation gives nominal oxygen mass flows of 0.93 and 1.86 mg/s. Only A2 recorded hot ignition, for two seconds before self-extinction. The original PSI table records approximate pressure of 2.2066 bar in both rows, while Appendix E of the dissertation reports nominal 2.0 atm. Direct conversion of 2.0 atm yields 2.0265 bar: the two values are different reported quantities. Keep the original field and qualifier with each value. Assigning the 85% to a habitat-atmosphere slider would promote a gas-burner test above a solid sample on a false match. [Kimber, methods on PDF pp. 20–21 and Table E.6 on PDF p. 62](https://api.drum.lib.umd.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/278c77a3-6e86-4dc5-8413-c0381ebe74a9/content#page=62), [PSI-159 inverse table, rows 18–19](https://doi.org/10.60555/cyt1-kh64)

**6. ICES-2025-392, test protocol, specimen and comparator.** Urban et al. changed conditions after ignition: the Glenn centrifuge group lowered local oxygen and the WSTF rig increased flow. Both used whether a flame survived a five-second window. At 8.2 psia the P213 tape result lies below WSTF’s forced-flow extrapolation. For polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro the paper describes lunar limits higher than the WSTF data. Preserve the wording of the comparator. P213 combines fiberglass with acrylic adhesive. Nomex Velcro has a different thickness and form from woven Nomex used in other studies. The authors discuss a possible shift onto the quenching branch and consider the relevant lunar buoyant velocity unknown. Their plotted positions do not constitute velocity measurements. ICES Fig. 13 and the single-material figures disagree on some lunar limits. FLINT uses Fig. 13, repeats the comparison with the alternate readings, and excludes cotton. Table 2 reports conservative differences obtained by extrapolating a worst-case slope from an assumed 35 cm/s at 1 g to zero; these are different from the observed lunar-minus-Earth differences. A separate study compared thin polycarbonate and Nomex under opposed flow in microgravity; its extrema occur under different flow and gravity. Transfer requires matching the comparison as well as the material. [Corrected paper, methods pp. 6–8, figures 8 and 11, discussion pp. 9–11 and Table 2](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20250002114/downloads/ICES_2025-392-correctedcaptions.pdf#page=8), [independent thin-polymer microgravity experiment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1540748918302852)

**7. FM², prediction with four dependent trials.** The March 2026 design supersedes a 2024 configuration involving two different fuels. On viewer p. 10 it specifies Synergy Pro Navy; the older shortlist table on viewer p. 14 calls one candidate Natural Synergy Pro. Confirm grade, finish and lot before joining a comparison. With a nominally common limiting oxygen concentration for the four specimens, outcomes are dependent and the effective sample size is small. A Brier score can compare predictions on resolved indices. It cannot establish calibration from one four-burn mission. NASA gives qualitative expectations and a 24–26% expected LOC. The guide's 26%/1.5 percentage-point distribution is a teaching assumption. A shared oxygen threshold assumes that sufficient starting oxygen will produce sustained spread after a functioning igniter. Registering a separate ignition model would be necessary to estimate a distinct ignition-failure probability. A nominal attempt with no ignition and an invalid igniter have different scoring dispositions. A changed design or missing footage can also make an observation unscorable. The April FY 2027 budget request plans FM² lunar work for 2027. These documents provide the design and planning basis; an official result with traceable per-burn outcomes is still needed for scoring. [Design and anticipated outcomes, PDF pp. 5–6 and 9–14](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20260001966/downloads/Ferkul-Lunar%20and%20Planetary%20Science%20Conf%202026%20v2.pdf#page=5), [NASA FM² overview](https://www.nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science/flammability-of-materials-on-the-moon-fm2/), [FY 2027 budget request](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/fiscal-year-2027-full-budget-request.pdf)

## Prior work and the choice of contribution

NASA PSI already provides originals, investigator metadata and persistent identifiers. PSI CSV rows, including rows that refer to a series rather than one physical burn, should remain the authority for what individual table cells mean. Correct captions, papers, images and apparatus records supply outcome definitions sometimes missing from the table. When a value is unavailable, zero would falsely look like a measured condition. An accession or DOI identifies a source; it cannot establish a count of independent experiments. [NASA PSI search](https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo), [NASA PSI investigator guide](https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/psi-database-guide.pdf)

MicroFire Atlas already describes mission ranking, source citations, evidence gaps, a model and a Saffire interface covering this very PMMA/Nomex case. Those features or the rediscovery of sample 2-7 would be weak originality claims. FIRST FIRE’s testable contribution is the ability to resolve materially different evidence questions with the right endpoint, comparator and measurement location, including cases where the correct response combines a positive finding with an unresolved transfer. Reserve any claim of time saved or higher user accuracy for a comparative participant study. [MicroFire Atlas repository](https://github.com/A-K-M-Asifuzzaman/MicroFire-Atlas), [its published Saffire interpretation](https://microfire-atlas.vercel.app/saffire)

The JAXA-led FLARE project, led by Osamu Fujita of Hokkaido University, already uses a ground-to-microgravity framework and low-speed forced-flow tests in the Kibo module. A 2026 primary study predicts an oxygen index of 18.6% for downward-spreading filter paper at 0.165 g and 56.5 kPa and compares the prediction with parabolic results. This prediction belongs to its filter paper and protocol. It shows how a matched experimental test can support a narrowly defined transfer. [JAXA FLARE](https://humans-in-space.jaxa.jp/en/biz-lab/experiment/theme/detail/000807.html), [JAXA investigator and publication record](https://humans-in-space.jaxa.jp/kibouser/pickout/73995.html), [partial-gravity filter-paper study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1540748926000957)

Oxygen enrichment has a physical analogue on Earth. A published surgical case records oxygen delivered by nasal catheter, an electric scalpel as ignition source and burning drapes. It supports the distinction between oxidizer, fuel and ignition source. Local gas composition near the drape was not reported; that case cannot quantify a lunar limiting oxygen concentration. [Original case report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22656688/)

## How to rank the alternatives

The case catalog ranks six ways to organize and validate evidence for each decision. Its first choice answers the immediate question with the fewest inferential steps. The middle choices make confounders, observable signals and counterexamples explicit. The final choices usually require unavailable imagery, a new experiment, labeled data or future mission results. These rankings guide design selection; a user ranking investigations by a particular scenario can legitimately obtain a different order. The full 42 trade-offs and their proof criteria are in [the case catalog](../data/cases.json).

| Case | Preferred organization | Cost of the shortcut it replaces | What verifies the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SIBAL | Separate base speed, tip speed and extinction in paired runs | A short experiment gets mistaken for a complete burn | Recover two slower rates and later extinction in the flight pair; withhold duration for the parabola |
| Saffire-II | Record each component and its position in the assembly | One outcome for the whole strip falsely transfers the PMMA burn to Nomex | Recover each component outcome at row 2-7 and preserve the soot caveat |
| FLEX | Represent visible and inferred combustion phases separately | Disappearance of light becomes an invented final-extinction label | Return different cool-phase judgments for 155 and 120 |
| SAME | Condition the detector response on aerosol source and measurement threshold | A smoke-generation setting is treated as a mission alarm time | Recover each reported fraction without manufacturing sample denominators |
| CFI-G | Bind composition to its burner or chamber location | 85% burner oxygen enters habitat-atmosphere matching | Exclude the inverse flame from the ambient-85%-oxygen textile subset |
| ICES | Name both material and Earth comparator in each signed result | A single sign or conservative margin is imposed on all materials | Recover opposite signs and preserve which one uses an extrapolation |
| FM² | Register separate event meanings before scoring | Chamber conditions, visual ignition and sustained spread are conflated | Keep forecast assumptions, invalid tests and eventual observations distinct |

## SI checks, evidentiary scope and study design

1. **Find supporting records.** Retrieve by fuel, phase, gravity regime, experiment identifier and requested endpoint. Run IDs, page numbers and material-grade strings are high-value exact matches. A semantic match on the word “oxygen” loses vital measurement context. Evidence close on partial pressure alone can be inappropriate for a flammability question. Report eligibility and mismatches ahead of any numeric distance. Test robustness by varying weights and dropping each dimension. Preserve tied alternatives and leave absent measurements blank.

2. **Check source occurrence.** Each quoted case passage has a source locator, a complete document SHA-256 and a sequence of token fingerprints calculated from the actual source page or published HTML section. The offline check tests the quotation against that page’s sequence. A stricter reproduction compares the entire source digest and regenerates the entire sequence independently with pypdf 6.10.0 or Python’s HTML parser. The four negative controls include a removed negation, altered duration, true words on a wrong page and a FLEX positive result misattributed to the inconclusive case. Source mismatch fails verification. The checks cover the ten marked quotations, not every paraphrase. [Verifier and commands](../data/evidence/README.md)

3. **Check interpretation.** A quotation may be real yet support only a narrower assertion. Treat each material, apparatus, endpoint, direction, gravity, oxygen location and valid comparator as part of a claim. A human reviewer can accept, qualify or reject the interpretation after reading the surrounding methods and caveat. None of the seven case judgments has been signed off by the user’s team. Retrieval scores, source match counts and generated text cannot be converted into a NASA probability or a new material qualification.

4. **Measure task performance.** Use a participant-blind answer key and randomized condition order. Rotate distinct but comparable cases between tools to limit recall. Record answer, source locator, elapsed time, unsupported conclusions and whether the participant explicitly abstained when appropriate. Keep recruitment, time and access conditions consistent. Where recruiting is possible, include the intended users and declare their number and experience. Demonstrating that an automated parser accepted a canned answer supplies no human usability result.

5. **Score the answer rather than overlap in words.** A four-point per-case rubric awards one point each for (a) correct endpoint and outcome, (b) correct source with run or page, (c) correct scope or comparison and (d) explicit unresolved transfer or alternative explanation. A blanket habitat safety verdict, reversed sign, fabricated measurement, invented team preregistration or forced outcome must be recorded as a critical error even when citation text matches. Report each task score and critical errors separately. If only one participant or a convenience sample is available, report their observed performance descriptively and avoid generalizing an effect.

6. **Keep decision and validation independent.** The public practice cases make the system inspectable. They cannot also be the unseen evaluation set used to claim scientific accuracy. Freeze the corpus and questions first, hold back entire investigations or material/protocol families for future generalization work, preserve completed/void/pending outcomes, and record misses. Candidate questions, architectures, acceptance conditions and published evidence are delivered now; new blind-user outcomes, measured improvement and independent preregistration require real observations or a team action.

## Remaining scientific gaps

Two comparisons address the learner guide’s questions about ventilation and sample size. In the Saffire-I flight, a 40.6 cm cotton–fiberglass strip burned for the allotted seven minutes and its flame went out when forced airflow stopped. In partial gravity, warmer gases can still rise and draw in oxidizer. NASA’s partial-gravity research update identifies that buoyant flow as a reason ventilation shutoff alone is ineffective there. The Saffire-I event supplies an orbital test observation. A crew response procedure would require the vehicle’s own validated guidance. [Saffire-I, PDF p. 16](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170008805/downloads/20170008805.pdf#page=16), [NASA materials flammability update, PDF p. 14](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20210021181/downloads/NASA%20Materials%20Flammability%20Update%20update%209.09.2021%20Final.pdf#page=14)

In Saffire-I and II, two samples of the same fabric spread at different rates in 20 cm/s concurrent flow. The 5 cm strip spread at 2.1 mm/s and the 40.6 cm strip at 1.8 mm/s. The smaller sample started at about 22.1% oxygen and the larger at 21.7%. The investigators also identified gas entering from the sides as a possible contributor. These measurements support testing width and initial oxygen separately. An earlier low-speed tunnel study likewise reported lower microgravity oxygen limits for some thin materials than under Earth upward-burn testing. Its spread-rate correlations were derived from a separate paper-wipe fuel, which matters when applying those correlations to flight fabrics. [Saffire rates and specimen conditions, PDF pp. 21 and 29](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170008805/downloads/20170008805.pdf#page=21), [Olson, Ruff and Miller, NASA/TM-2008-215260](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080034883)

* There is no matched, long-duration partial-gravity experiment here for every material, geometry and atmosphere. Oxygen enrichment and pressure act jointly with gravity-driven and forced flow. A ground cube-root velocity estimate is a conceptual scaling only; it cannot fill a missing velocity column.
* A five-second survival criterion can miss later extinction. Initial oxygen differs from oxygen at extinction when a chamber’s gas changes during a run. A drop-tower boundary, a full-length Test 1 pass and a proposed FM² event are distinct endpoints.
* BASS-II’s table provides genuine test provenance and gas measurements, but fan displays require instrument calibration before conversion to velocity. Closing a gap with a material’s name alone can join rods, sheets, adhesive or a woven fabric with different thermal behavior. [BASS-II NASA dataset](https://doi.org/10.60555/4qc4-de67)
* Similar oxygen partial pressures support neither an equivalence of all fire conditions nor a human-health determination; nitrogen concentration, pressure, heat loss and sample geometry matter. The NESC assessment describes engineering trade-offs at the programme level. [NASA NESC assessment](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20260003925)
* A score for this intervention requires an external case or independent participant. A time-stamped digest can prove which bytes existed at issuance; source presence and a hash of the guide’s worked example alone cannot prove when the team committed to its forecast.
